summary: This informational document describes an EPP domain name mapping extension for the provisioning and management of strict bundling registration of domain names, specified in XML. It states that this is a nonstandard proprietary extension.

plainLanguage.summary: Sometimes a set of similar domain names must be bought and kept together. This document explains one company's extra rules for handling such bundles through the registration protocol.

subtitle: Provisioning related domain names as an atomic group through EPP

tldr.problem: Domain name registries need to manage sets of related names (variants or different TLDs) as single units with shared properties, but the basic EPP domain mapping only handles individual domain names.
tldr.mechanism: This extension to EPP adds elements to represent bundled domain names (BDN) alongside registered domain names (RDN), allowing create, update, delete, and transfer operations to atomically affect all names in a bundle while they share attributes like expiry date and registrar.
tldr.outcome: Registries can now provision strict bundles where multiple names are created, renewed, transferred, and deleted together, maintaining consistency. This supports variant domain names in multiple languages and related TLDs under single ownership.

today: RFC 9095 is an Informational RFC describing a nonstandard EPP extension in use by registries managing bundled domain names, particularly those offering Chinese Domain Names and other internationalized variants. It provides interoperability documentation for registry software and registrars.

sections.title: Bundled Domains and Their Purpose
sections.content:
Bundled domain names are sets of related names that share attributes and must be managed together. Two types exist: variant-label bundles, where the second-level label differs (e.g., simplified and traditional Chinese versions of the same name in one TLD); and variant-TLD bundles, where the label is identical but the TLD differs (e.g., 'example.ngo' and 'example.ong', managed by the same entity).

The RFC focuses on strict bundling: all bundled names share the same expiry date, registrant, contacts, name servers, and status values. When one name is renewed, transferred, or updated, all bundled names change together atomically. This is essential for Chinese Domain Names (IDN variants) and other language-specific domains where variant forms must remain linked to the same owner.
sections.plainLanguage: A company wants to register 'myname.ngo' and 'myname.ong' together, and they always stay together. If one expires, both expire. If one is updated, both are updated.

sections.title: How EPP Bundled Registration Works
sections.content:
The registry accepts an EPP domain create request with one domain name—the RDN (Registered Domain Name). The registry then generates related bundled names according to policy and groups them as a bundle. All names in the bundle share a single domain object with unified properties.

When operations like check, info, create, update, delete, renew, or transfer are performed, the protocol must handle both the RDN and all BDNs (Bundled Domain Names) consistently. For example, checking the availability of one name returns the availability of all bundled names, and updating one updates all atomically. The extension ensures the registry can express this grouping in responses and handle it in commands.
sections.plainLanguage: The registrant registers one name, the system makes its bundles, and from then on they are treated as one unit by the registration system.

sections.title: EPP Commands for Bundles
sections.content:
The extension modifies EPP query and transform commands. For check and info, either the RDN or any BDN can be queried; the response includes all names in the bundle. For create, the client sends the RDN with an extension element that includes its U-label (Unicode display form); the registry generates BDNs and returns them. For delete, renew, transfer, and update, either the RDN or a BDN is accepted, and the operation applies to all bundled names.

The response includes RDN and BDN elements, each with an optional U-label attribute for readability. This allows clients and registries to see the Unicode form of internationalized domain names while the protocol carries the ASCII-compatible encoding (A-label) form.
sections.plainLanguage: Commands work on any name in the bundle and return all of them. You can ask about one, and the system tells you about all of them together.

sections.title: Support for Internationalized Domain Names
sections.content:
The extension is designed around IDN concepts. Domain names can be represented in two forms: the A-label (ASCII-compatible encoding, like 'xn--fsq270a.example') used in DNS, and the U-label (Unicode, like '实例.example') for human readability. The extension includes a 'uLabel' attribute on RDN and BDN elements so both forms are visible in protocol messages and responses.

This is especially important for Chinese Domain Names, where variant characters (Simplified vs. Traditional Chinese) represent the same semantic meaning. The registry can automatically generate variants as bundled names and expose their Unicode representation, making it clear to registrants which names are bundled.
sections.plainLanguage: Domain names in other languages are shown both as computer-readable codes and human-readable characters, so registrants can see what they are registering.

sections.title: Security and Shared Policies
sections.content:
The RFC notes that registries with 15+ years of bundled registration experience (especially in Chinese domains) have not reported significant security issues. The key principle is that registrants must understand that bundled names are created, transferred, updated, and deleted as a group—they cannot manage them independently.

A subtle point is that the RFC does not prescribe whether bundled names share DNSSEC keys. If they share the same Delegation Signer (DS) and DNS Public Key (DNSKEY) records, they share a common cryptographic fate: a key compromise affects all bundled names. Registries and DNS administrators can choose independent or shared keys based on their security model.
sections.plainLanguage: Bundled names should be owned by the same person. Registrants need to remember they move as a group. DNSSEC keys can be shared or separate, depending on what the registry decides.
